html:
Country stores and taverns of the Río de la Plata plains in the 1700s and after, where gauchos, the horsemen of the pampas, came to buy and drink. They were often the only shop for many kilometres.

A pulpería sold a little of everything: yerba mate, tobacco, sugar, salt, liquor, knives, cloth and horse gear. The shopkeeper served from behind an iron grille, for safety. Gauchos traded hides and tallow, the products of the plains, for what they needed, and gathered there to play cards, sing to the guitar, gamble and sometimes fight. Cart trains and mule drivers crossing the plains stopped there too.

The pulpería shows that trade and shops reached even remote frontiers. It also appears in gaucho poetry such as Martín Fierro. The name later passed to company stores in the nitrate mines of northern Chile, and pulperías still exist as small shops in parts of Latin America.
